title: How parliamentary immunity works in practice
seoTitle: How parliamentary immunity works in practice
subtitle: Understand the difference between protection for opinions and the rules for judicial proceedings involving federal lawmakers
excerpt: A detailed look at how parliamentary immunity works, its constitutional limits, political impacts, and the trial process at Brazil's Supreme Court.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
The institute of parliamentary immunity represents one of the most debated pillars of the Brazilian democratic framework, dividing opinions between the need to protect the legislative mandate and the pursuit of equality before the law. Far from being a personal privilege, this constitutional prerogative aims to ensure the free exercise of popular representation against external pressures and political persecution. Understanding how it works in practice is essential to deciphering the complex power relations that shape the daily life of the Republic.

The dual shielding of the legislative mandate in Brazil

The protection granted to holders of elective office at the federal level is divided into two fundamental and distinct aspects: material immunity and formal immunity. Both are enshrined in the constitutional text and have well-defined objectives to ensure that the Legislative Branch operates independently. Material immunity protects the essence of political activity—the debate of ideas—while formal immunity establishes specific rules for the processing of criminal proceedings against deputies and senators.

Material immunity dictates that lawmakers are inviolable, both civilly and criminally, for any of their opinions, words, and votes. In practice, this means that a deputy or senator cannot be prosecuted for injury, slander, or defamation due to statements made in the exercise of their office. However, the Federal Supreme Court has consolidated the understanding that this protection requires a functional link. In other words, statements must bear a direct relation to the parliamentary mandate, not covering offenses uttered in purely personal or private contexts.

On the other hand, formal immunity concerns procedural and arrest rules. It prevents federal lawmakers from being arrested from the moment of their electoral certification, except in cases of flagrant offenses for non-bailable crimes. Furthermore, formal immunity guarantees jurisdiction by prerogative of office, popularly known as privileged forum. This mechanism determines that criminal proceedings against deputies and senators be tried directly by the Supreme Court, preventing first-instance judges from arbitrarily interfering with the functioning of the National Congress.

The historical roots of protection for lawmakers

The need to protect elected representatives dates back to the historical conflicts between Parliament and the Crown in England, as far back as the late 17th century. At that time, the monarch used the judiciary to arrest and prosecute lawmakers who opposed royal decisions. The consecration of the principle that discussions held within Parliament could not be questioned in external courts was a crucial milestone for the birth of modern constitutionalism and the consolidation of the separation of powers.

With the French Revolution in the late 18th century, the concept took on a new guise. The revolutionaries realized that without formal protection against arbitrary arrests, the legislative assembly could be hollowed out by the executive branch at any moment. Thus, the physical inviolability of lawmakers was established, ensuring that the lawmaking process was not interrupted by politically motivated persecution. This model influenced Western democracies and was incorporated by subsequent constitutions around the world.

In Brazil, parliamentary immunity has been present since the first Constitution of the Empire, granted in the first half of the nineteenth century. Throughout republican history, the scope of these guarantees has fluctuated according to the prevailing political regime. During authoritarian periods, such as the mid-twentieth century, prerogatives were suspended or drastically reduced, allowing for the revocation of mandates and the imprisonment of opponents. With redemocratization in the late 1980s, the current National Constituent Assembly broadly reestablished these guarantees, aiming to shield Parliament against new democratic regressions.

The process for prosecuting a lawmaker in the justice system

The course of a criminal investigation against a federal deputy or senator follows a rigorous procedure distinct from that applied to ordinary citizens. The process begins under the direct supervision of the Federal Supreme Court, which oversees all stages of evidence gathering. If the Prosecutor General's Office finds sufficient evidence of authorship and materiality of a common crime, it files a formal indictment before the Supreme Court.

Following the presentation of the indictment, the lawmaker has the opportunity to present a preliminary defense. The Plenary or one of the panels of the Federal Supreme Court analyzes the arguments and decides whether to accept or reject the indictment. If the accusation is accepted, the lawmaker becomes a defendant, and the procedural instruction phase begins, featuring witness testimonies and expert examinations. This entire process is governed by the Code of Criminal Procedure, but with acts centralized in the higher court.

The situation takes on high-voltage political undertones when a lawmaker is caught in flagrante delicto for a non-bailable crime. Under these circumstances, the Federal Supreme Court must record the flagrant arrest and forward the case files the following day to the respective legislative house—either the Chamber of Deputies or the Federal Senate. It is then up to the members of that house to analyze the legality and necessity of the arrest. In an open session, lawmakers vote publicly to decide whether to keep their colleague detained or order their immediate release.

The scope of special jurisdiction in numbers and cases

The volume of cases involving authorities with special jurisdiction has always been at the center of debates regarding the efficiency of Brazilian criminal justice. The Federal Supreme Court notes in its historical reports that, prior to the interpretive changes made to the structure of this jurisdiction, the court accumulated hundreds of inquiries and criminal actions against lawmakers. This accumulation created operational bottlenecks, since higher courts are not originally structured to conduct the instruction phase of common crimes.

The Getulio Vargas Foundation published detailed data showing that the processing of criminal actions against holders of special jurisdiction in the Supreme Court tended to be slower than in the first instance, due to the court's accumulated constitutional duties. This reality prompted a drastic shift in interpretation in the late 2010s. Based on a landmark ruling, the Federal Supreme Court restricted the scope of jurisdiction by prerogative of office, establishing that it applies only to crimes committed in the exercise of the mandate and bearing a direct relation to parliamentary duties.

The Judicial Research Department of the National Council of Justice demonstrates that this restriction resulted in a sharp decline in the number of ongoing cases in the country's highest court. Hundreds of inquiries investigating events prior to taking office or unrelated to legislative activity were forwarded to first-instance judges across the national territory. This movement decentralized investigations and allowed the Supreme Court to focus primarily on its constitutional review duties.

The most common misconceptions about privileged jurisdiction

There are a series of mistaken interpretations that distort the real nature of parliamentary immunity in public opinion. The most frequent error is associating special jurisdiction with automatic impunity. In reality, the special forum merely alters the competent judging body, transferring the case to a top-tier collegiate court. Lawmakers remain subject to the penalties set forth in the Penal Code, including prison sentences, provided they are convicted after due process of law.

Another common myth is believing that immunity protects lawmakers in civil or administrative actions. Material immunity and special jurisdiction apply strictly to the criminal sphere. Proceedings involving contract disputes, family law, debt collection, or even administrative misconduct actions proceed normally in ordinary first-instance courts. A deputy can be ordered to pay damages for moral harm or have assets frozen by a single judge without violating their legislative prerogatives.

It is also incorrect to assume that parliamentary immunity is a lifelong right. Protection is strictly tied to the exercise of political mandate. The moment a lawmaker leaves office, whether due to the end of their elected term, resignation, or the revocation of their mandate, they immediately lose the right to special jurisdiction. All inquiries and ongoing proceedings in the Federal Supreme Court that are not in their final trial phase are declined to ordinary justice, where the former lawmaker will answer like any other citizen.

How the balance between powers affects the ordinary citizen

Although it may seem like a topic far removed from everyday reality, the functioning of parliamentary immunity has a direct impact on the life of every voter. The system of checks and balances, which underpins the equilibrium between the Executive, Legislative, and Judiciary branches, relies on these guarantees to prevent abuses of power. Without material immunity, an opposition lawmaker could be constantly prosecuted for exposing corruption schemes or criticizing the public policies of incumbent rulers, silencing the voice of those who represent significant portions of the population.

On the other hand, the distortion of these guarantees fosters a sense of injustice that erodes citizen trust in democratic institutions. When immunity is used as a shield to protect property crimes, the diversion of public funds, or systemic corruption, society perceives the mechanism as an affront to the republican principle that all are equal before the law. Therefore, the search for a point of equilibrium is constant in national legal history.

Thus, the ordinary citizen is affected by both the lack and the excess of protection for their representatives. A weakened parliament fearing judicial retaliation cannot fulfill its role of overseeing government actions and legislating independently on controversial topics. At the same time, a parliament shielded from any criminal accountability distances itself from society's ethical demands, undermining the legitimacy of the democratic regime itself.

Questions citizens ask about immunity

Can a lawmaker be prosecuted for crimes committed before taking office?

Yes. If the crime was committed before taking office and has no relation to parliamentary activity, the proceeding must be processed in the first instance of ordinary justice. Taking office does not automatically attract these old proceedings to the Federal Supreme Court, in accordance with the forum restriction rules established by current constitutional jurisprudence.

What happens if a deputy is criminally convicted?

If the criminal conviction is final, with no possibility of further appeals, the Federal Supreme Court communicates the decision to the board of directors of the respective legislative house. Depending on the prison regime imposed and the nature of the crime, the loss of the mandate will be declared by the board of directors or submitted to a vote by the plenary of the house, which will decide on the final revocation of the political office.

Do city councilors have the same level of protection as federal deputies?

No. City councilors possess only material immunity, which guarantees inviolability for their opinions, words, and votes, but with strict geographic limitation: this protection is only valid within the limits of the municipality where they hold office. Furthermore, city councilors do not have formal immunity against arrest and do not possess special jurisdiction in the Federal Supreme Court, being tried by state ordinary justice.

Does immunity protect against the loss of a mandate for breach of parliamentary decorum?

No. Parliamentary immunity does not prevent legislative houses from initiating internal proceedings to investigate ethical misconduct or breaches of parliamentary decorum. The ethics committees of the Chamber of Deputies and the Federal Senate have the autonomy to investigate the behavior of their members and propose punishments ranging from reprimands to the revocation of the mandate, regardless of whether there is a judicial conviction.

The debate on improving constitutional guarantees

The debate surrounding the limits of parliamentary immunity and jurisdiction by prerogative of office remains active in the national political arena. There are currents advocating for the complete abolition of the special forum for common crimes, arguing that the measure would bring the people's representatives closer to the reality faced by ordinary citizens in first-instance courts. This constitutional amendment proposal is seen by defenders of legal equality as a necessary step for modernizing Brazilian institutions.

Conversely, jurists and institutional analysts warn of the risks of totally eliminating these guarantees in a country with deep regional political divisions. The fear is that, without the technical and centralized filter of the Federal Supreme Court, federal lawmakers could become easy targets for judicial decisions coordinated by local political adversaries, compromising governmental stability and national representation. Preserving the independence of lawmakers is seen, in this respect, as a safeguard against authoritarianism.

The improvement of this mechanism lies, therefore, in the rigorous application of the limits already established by jurisprudence and in the transparent conduct of legislative houses when analyzing the ethical behavior of their members. Parliamentary immunity fulfills its democratic role when it protects the institution of Parliament and the sovereignty of the popular vote, and not when it is converted into an individual safeguard against the application of justice. The equilibrium of this system is what ensures the strength of republican institutions in the long run.
